questions.text:
Consider a single processor system with four processes A, B, C, and D, represented as given below, where for each process the first value is its arrival time, and the second value is its CPU burst time.

A (0, 10), B (2, 6), C (4, 3), and D (6, 7).

Which one of the following options gives the average waiting times when preemptive Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) and Non-Preemptive Shortest Job First (NP-SJF) CPU scheduling algorithms are applied to the processes?
questions.solution:
SRTF Gantt chart: A(0-2), B(2-4), C(4-7), B(7-11), D(11-18), A(18-26)
Waiting = completion [latex]-[/latex] arrival [latex]-[/latex] burst:
A = 26[latex]-[/latex]0[latex]-[/latex]10 = 16, B = 11[latex]-[/latex]2[latex]-[/latex]6 = 3, C = 7[latex]-[/latex]4[latex]-[/latex]3 = 0, D = 18[latex]-[/latex]6[latex]-[/latex]7 = 5
Average [latex]=24/4=6[/latex]

NP-SJF Gantt chart: A(0-10), C(10-13), B(13-19), D(19-26)
Waiting: A = 0, C = 10[latex]-[/latex]4 = 6, B = 13[latex]-[/latex]2 = 11, D = 19[latex]-[/latex]6 = 13
Average [latex]=30/4=7.5[/latex]

Answer: SRTF = 6, NP-SJF = 7.5

questions.text: Which  one  of  the  following  CIDR  prefixes  exactly  represents  the  range  of IP addresses 10.12.2.0 to 10.12.3.255?
questions.solution:
10.12.2.0 to 10.12.3.255 has [latex]2\times256=512=2^9[/latex] addresses, so host bits = 9 and prefix = [latex]32-9=23[/latex].

Third octet: 2 = 00000010, 3 = 00000011 [latex]\text{---}[/latex] the first 23 bits are the same, so the block is aligned.

(/24 covers only 10.12.2.x; /22 covers 10.12.0.0-10.12.3.255.)

Answer: 10.12.2.0/23

questions.text:
You are given a set [latex]V[/latex] of distinct integers. A binary search tree [latex]T[/latex] is created by inserting all elements of [latex]V[/latex] one by one, starting with an empty tree. The tree [latex]T[/latex] follows the convention that, at each node, all values stored in the left subtree of the node are smaller than the value stored at the node. You are not aware of the sequence in which these values were inserted into [latex]T[/latex], and you do not have access to [latex]T[/latex].
Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.solution:
The inorder traversal of any BST is the keys in sorted order, whatever the insertion order. So it can be found from V just by sorting.

Root, preorder and postorder depend on the insertion order. Example V = {1, 2}: inserting 1 then 2 gives root 1; inserting 2 then 1 gives root 2.

Answer: Inorder traversal of T can be determined from V

questions.text:
Consider the following context-free grammar where the start symbol is [latex] S [/latex] and the set of terminals is [latex] \{a, b, c, d\} [/latex].

[latex] \begin{aligned} & S \rightarrow A a A b \mid B b B a \\ & A \rightarrow c S \mid \epsilon \\ & B \rightarrow d S \mid \epsilon \end{aligned} [/latex]

The following is a partially-filled LL(1) parsing table.

[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline & a & b & c & d & \$ \\ \hline S & S \rightarrow A a A b & S \rightarrow B b B a & (1) & (2) & \\ \hline A & A \rightarrow \epsilon & (3) & A \rightarrow c S & & \\ \hline B & (4) & B \rightarrow \epsilon & & B \rightarrow d S & \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]

Which one of the following options represents the CORRECT combination for the numbered cells in the parsing table?
Note: In the options, "blank" denotes that the corresponding cell is empty.
questions.solution:
Fill the LL(1) table using FIRST and FOLLOW sets:
- [latex]FIRST(AaAb)=\{c,a\}[/latex] (A is c[latex]\ldots[/latex] or [latex]\epsilon[/latex]) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] cell (1) [S, c] = [latex]S\rightarrow AaAb[/latex].
- [latex]FIRST(BbBa)=\{d,b\}[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] cell (2) [S, d] = [latex]S\rightarrow BbBa[/latex].
- [latex]A\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex] goes under FOLLOW(A). A appears before a and before b, so [latex]FOLLOW(A)\supseteq\{a,b\}[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] cell (3) [A, b] = [latex]A\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex].
- Similarly [latex]FOLLOW(B)\supseteq\{b,a\}[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] cell (4) [B, a] = [latex]B\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex].

Answer: (1) [latex]S\rightarrow AaAb[/latex] (2) [latex]S\rightarrow BbBa[/latex] (3) [latex]A\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex] (4) [latex]B\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex]
